body: When I was young I thought all fathers had a chair like this: a place in the house that was unmistakably theirs, that the rest of us orbited rather than occupied.

He died on a Tuesday in March, and for a long time nobody in the house could sit in that chair. It just sat there, blue and empty and somehow still fully his, the way a coat still holds the shape of the person who wore it last.

It was my mother who finally sat in it, almost a year later, on a Friday evening before the candles were lit. She didn't say anything about it. She just sat down the way you'd sit in any chair, picked up the remote, and watched the news the way he used to — arguing quietly with the anchor under her breath.
Nobody in the family has ever gotten rid of that chair. It's still blue. It's still ugly. The dent in the armrest is still there, a little deeper now, holding two shapes instead of one.
lead: There was a recliner in the corner of the den that my father called his office, though as far as any of us could tell, the only business conducted there was arguing with the evening news and falling asleep before Wheel of Fortune finished. It was the color of a swimming pool on a postcard — a blue nobody would have chosen on purpose, which is probably why he loved it. My mother tried to replace it three times over twenty years. Three times it came back from the curb, carried in by my father like a man rescuing a dog from a shelter. The chair had a permanent dent shaped like him — a groove worn into the right armrest where his watch used to click against the wood trim while he read the paper.

body: Harlan did it.

With Ancestry, raw persistence, fierce curiosity, and far more patience than most people could ever muster, Harlan reopened a branch of our family history that had been lost, scattered, and disconnected for decades.
At the time, we wrote:
L'Dor V'Dor — from generation to generation.
What we didn't fully realize then was that Harlan hadn't actually finished the family tree.
He had done something better.
He gave us the trail so we could keep walking it.
And this week, we followed that trail a little farther into the past.
Beyond the Man in the Buggy
For years, the man in this old photograph was basically just that:
"The man in the buggy."
We had a name — Julius Yaffe, our paternal great-grandfather.
We had the image of him in a suit and hat, sitting behind a well-groomed horse in what appears to be an open surrey carriage.
We had some dates.
Some names.
A few scattered branches on a digital family tree.
But Julius died in March 1942, long before we were born.
His son Harry Yaffe — our paternal grandfather — was also gone before either Harlan or I entered the world.
Think about the silence created by that gap.
We were born already missing two entire generations of firsthand paternal family memory.
We could never sit down with Grandpa Harry and ask the everyday questions:
What was your father Julius really like?
Did he have an accent?
Was he strict, or did he laugh easily?
What did he tell you about the old country?
What did he do for a living?
And we certainly couldn't ask Julius the questions that burn a little brighter now:
Where exactly were you born?
Why did you leave?
What was the voyage to America like?
What did America look like through your eyes when you first arrived?
Were you scared?
Were you excited?
And yes...
Was that actually your horse?
Those voices were already gone.
Which is why what we found this week feels so meaningful.
Two Words Carved in Stone
We located Julius's gravestone in New Jersey.
Above the English inscription, his identity is preserved in Hebrew:
Yehudah ben Avraham Yitzchak
Judah, son of Abraham Isaac.
Beneath it:

BELOVED FATHER
JULIUS YAFFE
DIED MAR. 17, 1942
AGE 78 YRS
But after all the dates and genealogical details, it was those first two English words that made us stop:
BELOVED FATHER
Someone chose those words.
His children knew the man we are now trying to piece back together.
They knew the cadence of his voice.
They knew what made him angry and what made him smile.
They knew what it felt like to sit at his dinner table.
They knew stories about him that no census taker, immigration official, or newspaper could ever record.
And when it came time to summarize his life in stone, they didn't choose:

Immigrant.
Russian.
Lithuanian.
Businessman.
American.
Successful.
They chose:
Beloved Father.
And the line continued:

Julius Yaffe — Yehudah ben Avraham Yitzchak
Harry Yaffe
Our Father
Harlan and me
L'Dor V'Dor.
The Beautiful Friction of the Past
This research is also teaching us something important:
Family history rarely moves in a perfectly straight line.
Six months ago, the best information we had placed Julius's birth in Pandėlys, in what is now Lithuania, in 1862.
Other family records we have uncovered point instead toward Smolensk, Russia.
The older family tree identified his father as Yitzhok Yaffe.
His gravestone gives us Avraham Yitzchak.
The family tree gives Julius a birth year of 1862, while the gravestone says he was 78 when he died in 1942, suggesting his birth may have been closer to 1863 or 1864.
Those questions are not failures in the research.
They are the research.
Genealogy isn't a perfectly bound history book waiting for someone to open it.
We inherit fragments.
A photograph someone managed not to lose.
A name passed down through several generations.
A handwritten census entry faded by time.
A marriage record.
An old newspaper advertisement.
A gravestone in a quiet cemetery.
Sometimes the pieces fit perfectly.
Sometimes they argue with each other.
And almost every answer creates two new questions.
But the fog is clearing.
We can now see Julius's wife, Liba, and the names of their children appearing in the records — including Morris, Harry, William and Mary, with more pieces still being sorted out.
Harry, of course, is the anchor for our branch.
From the coastal communities around Belmar, New Jersey, Harry's path eventually led to Toledo, Ohio, where the next chapters of the Yaffe story were written.
And that is where genealogy stops feeling ancient.
Because that line eventually reaches Dad.
Then Harlan and me.
Then our children.
And the generations still to come.
L'Dor V'Dor.
A Witness to an Extraordinary Transformation
Looking at that buggy photograph now, the timeline is almost impossible to comprehend.
Julius was born in the early 1860s.
He entered a world of horses, steam, oil lamps and handwritten letters.
He lived to see electric lighting transform cities.
The telephone.
Motion pictures.
The automobile.
The Wright brothers take flight.
Radio bridge enormous distances.
He lived through World War I.
The 1918 influenza pandemic.
The Great Depression.
And he lived just long enough to see America enter World War II after Pearl Harbor.
Julius died on March 17, 1942.
Imagine the distance between the world into which that little Jewish boy was born in the Russian Empire and the America in which that old man closed his eyes.
The horse and carriage in the photograph would eventually give way to automobiles.
Letters crossing oceans would give way to voices traveling through the air.
Entire countries would disappear and borders would be redrawn.
And somewhere in the middle of that enormous changing world...
our family happened.
The Command to Remember
This week's Torah portion, Eikev, repeatedly returns to the importance of remembering the journey.
Do not become so comfortable with where you are that you forget the difficult road that brought you there.
That message feels especially powerful this week.
Remembering isn't simply memorizing names on a family tree.
It is understanding that our lives began long before we drew our first breath.
People we never met made choices that eventually made our lives possible.
They packed bags.
Crossed borders.
Crossed oceans.
Started over.
Found work.
Built businesses.
Raised children.
Buried people they loved.
Took chances.
Failed.
Tried again.
And somehow kept the next generation moving forward.
Eventually...
there was us.
Which Brings Us Back to Harlan
For seven years, these weekly Shabbat Shalom stories have helped make sure that Harlan never becomes a sterile record:

Harlan Blaine Yaffe
Born...
Died...
and an old photograph someone finds eighty years from now.
We know too much to let that happen.
We know the punchlines.
The businesses.
The favorite restaurants.
The childhood scrapes.
The stubborn arguments.
The private conversations.
The people he quietly helped.
We remember Mom and Dad.
We remember growing up.
We remember things that seemed completely ordinary when they happened.
And we keep returning to Harlan's message:
Peace, Love & Equality for all.
Those ordinary stories are exactly what we wish we had from Julius and Harry today.
We cannot ask Grandpa Harry.
We cannot ask Julius.
And now we cannot ask Harlan.
But there is one very important difference:
Harlan asked.
He dug.
He searched.
He called.
He connected cousins.
He followed names into forgotten branches.
He helped reconnect generations of a family that had drifted apart.
And most importantly, he left us enough breadcrumbs to keep going.
Six months ago, we said:
Harlan did it.
Today, we understand those words a little differently.
Harlan didn't finish the family tree.
He made sure the tree was still alive.
He gave us a trail.
And because he did, more than 84 years after Julius Yaffe died, the man in the buggy is slowly becoming a person again.
Not just a faded face in an old photograph.
Not just Julius Yaffe.
But:
Yehudah ben Avraham Yitzchak.
Our great-grandfather.
Harry's father.
One link in a chain that eventually reached us.
And according to the people who actually knew him, sat beside him, argued with him, laughed with him, loved him and missed him...
A Beloved Father.
May we keep asking the questions.
May we preserve the answers we are fortunate enough to find.
May we correct the story when new evidence teaches us something new.
And may we leave the generations who follow us a clearer map of where they came from than the one we inherited.
L'Dor V'Dor.
Shabbat Shalom.

body: Back then, if you packed it, you carried it.
In an earlier #HarlansLegacy post, we wrote about the small travel case that once held our comic books. Over the past 387 weeks, we have also written many times about Harlan’s travels.
He went to trade shows and industry conventions. He traveled to support his team and to receive crystal plaques, awards, and recognition for their advanced digital artistry.
This week’s photograph is of another part of that story: Harlan’s red SwissGear suitcase.
It traveled with him to Curaçao, Ibiza, Amsterdam, and many other places along the way.
When that dreadful day came and I had to pack one suitcase with some of Harlan’s possessions, this was the suitcase I chose.
For most of the past seven years, I continued using it during my own road-warrior travels.
It carried my clothes from state to state, but it also carried something much more important.
It carried memories.

In those early days, it helped stabilize my mental state. It comforted me during my state of denial. It stayed beside me through the different states of grief—and then followed me into the next state.
It was something familiar from Harlan’s life that I could still take with me.
His luggage tag is still attached.
It has an address that has long been vacant, a telephone number that has been disconnected, and an email account that is no longer active.
But it still has Harlan’s name.
Eventually, however, the suitcase began showing its age. The miles had taken their toll, and it was no longer suitable for the road.
As I write this week’s Shabbat Shalom post from the great state of Wisconsin, Harlan’s red suitcase did not make the trip.
Its traveling days are now over.
It is now safely at home, filled with family heirlooms, keepsakes, and pieces of Harlan’s legacy—zipped tightly and secured for posterity.
That brings us to this week’s Torah portion, Re’eh, which means “See.”
It asks us to do more than simply look at what is in front of us. It asks us to recognize what something truly represents.
Someone else may look at this photograph and see an old, worn red suitcase.
I see the places Harlan traveled.
I see the work he was proud of and the people whose accomplishments he celebrated.
I see the terrible day when I packed some of his possessions inside it.
Each week, we open another part of our family’s story. We remember Harlan, our mom and dad, their parents, and the generations who came before them.
This week, we zip one small chapter closed.
Farewell to the road, old red suitcase.
You carried Harlan’s belongings around the world.
You carried some of them home.
And when I needed it most, you helped carry me.
Your traveling days may be finished.
Your place in #HarlansLegacy is not.
Shabbat Shalom.

body: “Justice, justice shall you pursue.”
Why repeat the word justice?

Perhaps because justice isn’t only about deciding who is right and who is wrong. It is also about being willing to look honestly at ourselves—to recognize our own actions, our own responsibilities, and our own shortcomings.
There is an interesting parallel in the New Testament, where Jesus teaches that before we concern ourselves with the fault in another person, we should first examine the fault within ourselves.
Different traditions, but a remarkably similar lesson:
Justice in the world begins with accountability in our own hearts.
And that brings me back to one of my favorite childhood memories of my brother, Harlan—and to a lesson our parents may have taught us without ever realizing they were teaching it.

There was a time when Harlan and I were probably six and eight—or maybe eight and ten. We were both still in grade school, and for some reason, children had discovered the magical world of ballpoint-pen tattoos.
You know the kind.
A kid takes an ordinary ink pen and draws a flower, a name, or some mysterious artwork on their arm and proudly announces, “Look! I have a tattoo!”
Our mother, God bless her, was what we affectionately called a Nervous Nelly. She was convinced that the ink would somehow work its way through our skin, enter our bloodstream, and poison us.
Therefore, under no circumstances were Harlan or I permitted to draw on ourselves with ink pens.
And then I watched my big brother get caught.
Harlan got in trouble.
And I was the innocent little brother, standing safely on the sidelines, watching and learning.
Or so Mom and Dad thought.
A day or two later, I was at school talking with a classmate about what had happened to Harlan. Somehow, in the course of that conversation, my friend drew a little flower on my arm.
I had my tattoo.
Then I forgot about it.
Until bath time.
Somehow, Mom or Dad noticed the ink on my skin.
“Hal, what’s that?”
Now, I was young. Too young to understand one of the great mysteries of childhood:
How do parents always know when you’re lying?
So I put on my best politician’s face and delivered what I thought was an absolutely airtight explanation.
“No. There was a problem in class. The ink pen blew up and exploded, and the ink got on my arm.”
I said it with a perfectly straight face.
I fully expected to be believed.
Instead, Mom and Dad looked at each other.
They didn’t say anything.
They didn’t even roll their eyes.
They just exchanged that mysterious parental look—the secret language parents apparently learn when their child is standing three feet away telling the most ridiculous lie they have ever heard.
And somehow…they let me get away with it.
A few years later, the subject came up again.
Dad’s fraternity brother, Uncle Merill Janowitz, owner of People Pawn on Monroe Street, was like an uncle to us.
For some reason, Mom and Dad were in the back of the house getting ready, and Uncle Merle was up front with Harlan and me.
Uncle Merle picked up an ink pen and drew a little heart on my tush.
Of course, Mom and Dad eventually saw it and laughed till the end.
I couldn’t even reach that spot!
I looked at them and essentially argued my case like a miniature attorney:
“I didn’t do it. Uncle Merle did!”
And Uncle Merle, to his credit, owned it.
He admitted that he had drawn the heart.
Case dismissed.
I was not shipped off to reform school for my violent and blatant disregard of parental authority.
And maybe there is a reason neither Harlan nor I ever got a tattoo.
Maybe it was because Mom had successfully scared the ink right out of us.
Maybe it was because neither of us particularly liked needles.
Maybe it was because neither of us had any desire to turn our bodies into permanent canvases.
Or perhaps, in some strange way, our parents’ lesson simply stuck.
They were both free of ink, too!
Three different times I remember ink pens making Mom and Dad furious.
And to Harlan’s dying day, neither of us ever used indelible ink on ourselves.
Harlan might eventually have chosen a Waterman or a Montblanc.
But neither of us ever chose a tattoo needle.
Looking back now, I realize there was another lesson hidden inside those childhood memories.
Our parents weren’t simply teaching us what not to do.
They were teaching us about accountability.
Sometimes we argued.
Sometimes we tried to outsmart them.
Sometimes we even invented exploding ink pens.
But eventually we learned that the easiest person to fool is ourselves.
And perhaps that is what “Justice, justice shall you pursue” asks of us.
Before we point a finger, look inward.
Before we decide who is wrong, ask what part we played.
Before we demand accountability from someone else, have the courage to practice it ourselves.

We don’t always understand those lessons when we are children. Sometimes they arrive disguised as parental rules, childhood arguments, embarrassing stories, or even a ridiculous explanation about an exploding ink pen.
But years later, we discover that something stayed with us.
Not necessarily the rule itself—but the deeper lesson behind it.
Pursue justice in the world—but begin by practicing it in your own heart.
Because ultimately, we cannot make the world more just without making our own hearts more just.
That is a lesson worth carrying forward.
A lesson worth remembering.
A lesson worth leaving as part of our legacy.
And perhaps that is part of Harlan’s legacy too—not simply the memories of the things we did together, but the lessons we carried forward from the family that raised us.
Some lessons came through words.
Some came through consequences.
And some came through a little ink, a childhood lie, an exploding pen…and a heart drawn by Uncle Merill.
Perhaps someday I’ll get “Peace, Love and Equality for all!” tatted on my chest!
